content: In the genetic code, a stop codon, also known as a termination codon, is a specific sequence of three nucleotides within messenger RNA (mRNA) that signals the end of the translation process. Proteins are composed of unique sequences of amino acids, and during translation, most codons in mRNA direct the addition of specific amino acids to the growing polypeptide chain. However, stop codons serve a different function by halting this process, leading to the release of the completed polypeptide chain from the ribosome. In the standard genetic code, there are three stop codons: UAG, referred to as amber; UAA, known as ochre; and UGA, called opal or umber. While these three are the most common stop codons, variations in the genetic code can result in alternative sets of stop codons. A nonsense mutation is a type of genetic mutation in which a premature stop codon is introduced into the DNA sequence. This results in the production of an abnormally truncated protein, as translation is terminated earlier than intended. Such truncated proteins often lose their normal function because critical regions of the amino acid sequence are not synthesized. Due to this association with premature termination, stop codons are sometimes referred to as nonsense codons. Historically, the three stop codons were given distinct names—amber, ochre, and opal—based on their discovery and the specific types of mutants they were associated with. These mutants were initially identified in bacteriophages, such as T4 and lambda, which are viruses that infect the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli). Mutations in the viral genes often reduced the ability of the viruses to infect bacteria, and in some cases, the viruses could only infect specific strains of E. coli. The amber mutation was the first nonsense mutation to be discovered. It was identified by Harris Bernstein, a graduate student, during experiments aimed at resolving a scientific debate between Richard Epstein and Charles Steinberg. Bernstein’s last name, which means amber in German, was used to name this class of mutations. Amber mutations are characterized by their ability to infect certain strains of bacteria known as amber suppressors. These bacteria carry their own mutations, such as alterations in transfer RNA (tRNA), which allow them to bypass the effects of the amber stop codon. For instance, a mutation in the tRNA that recognizes the amber stop codon enables the ribosome to read through the stop signal, allowing translation to continue and produce a full-length protein. This process restores the normal function of the protein and effectively suppresses the amber mutation. As a result, amber mutants represent a class of viral mutants that can grow in bacteria containing amber suppressor mutations. The ochre mutation was the second nonsense mutation to be identified. To maintain the color-based naming convention established with amber, this mutation was named ochre. Like amber mutants, ochre mutants also regained their ability to infect bacteria when grown in specific suppressor strains. However, the suppressor strains that restored function to ochre mutants were distinct from those that suppressed amber mutations. This distinction suggested that ochre mutations corresponded to a different nucleotide triplet. Through a series of experiments comparing amber and ochre mutants with each other and with codons for known amino acids, Sydney Brenner determined that the amber and ochre stop codons corresponded to the nucleotide triplets UAG and UAA, respectively. The third and final stop codon in the standard genetic code, UGA, was discovered shortly thereafter. Nonsense mutations that introduced this premature stop codon were later referred to as opal mutations or umber mutations.
